children.text: Most bad regime decisions do not come from wrong arithmetic. They come from a sentence someone heard in the office canteen, a family WhatsApp group or an insurance agent's pitch. This lesson collects the myths and mistakes that cost Indian taxpayers the most, and gives you the one-line correction for each, drawn from everything you have already learned.

body.text: Every regime myth survives because it was once true, is sometimes true, or sounds true. The only defence is to run your own numbers every year.

body.caption: Regime Myths vs Reality, Tax Year 2026-27

cells: The old regime is always better for salaried people
Up to ₹12.75 lakh of salary it can only tie, and above that it needs ₹5 lakh to ₹8 lakh of benefits beyond the standard deduction
Chapter 3, Lesson 2
Income up to ₹12 lakh is always tax-free
Only for residents, and the rebate does not cover special-rate income like short-term gains on shares
Chapter 3, Lesson 4
The new regime has no deductions at all
Standard deduction of ₹75,000, employer NPS up to 14% of basic, and retirement and capital gains exemptions all survive
Chapter 2, Lesson 3
A raise into a higher slab cuts take-home pay
Only income above each threshold is taxed at the higher rate, and marginal relief protects you just above ₹12 lakh
Chapter 1, Lesson 2
The regime I told HR is final
For salaried taxpayers without business income, the return decides
Chapter 4, Lessons 1 and 3
Once you pick a regime you are stuck forever
Only taxpayers with business income face switching limits; others choose every year
Chapter 4, Lesson 2
ELSS and insurance save tax whatever regime you are in
80C deductions exist only in the old regime
Chapter 2, Lesson 1
In the new regime you should stop investing
The regime changes your tax, not your need for insurance, retirement savings or an emergency fund
Chapter 2, Lesson 1
Senior citizens should always choose the old regime
Their higher exemption limit helps, but the new regime's ₹12 lakh rebate often beats it
Chapter 2, Lesson 3

body.title: Myth Buster: Who Pays Nil Tax?
body.question: All four use the new regime in tax year 2026-27. Who pays zero tax?
options: Ankit, resident: salary ₹11,50,000 plus ₹60,000 short-term gains on shares
Bela, resident: salary ₹12,00,000 plus ₹60,000 of dividends
Chetan, resident: salary ₹13,50,000 and no other income
Dinesh, NRI: ₹10,00,000 of interest from NRO deposits in India
body.explanation: Bela's taxable income is ₹12,00,000 minus ₹75,000 plus ₹60,000, which is ₹11,85,000. Dividends are taxed at slab rates, so the rebate covers them in full. Ankit's rebate cannot touch the 20% tax on his short-term gains. Chetan's taxable income of ₹12,75,000 is past the marginal relief zone, so he pays ₹71,250 plus cess. Dinesh is an NRI and cannot claim the rebate at all.

body.title: Myth Buster: The Promotion
body.question: Kavitha's salary rises from ₹12,50,000 to ₹13,00,000 under the new regime. Her tax goes from nil to ₹26,000. Which statement is correct?
options: She is ₹26,000 worse off than before the raise
She is ₹24,000 better off, because marginal relief limits her tax to the income above ₹12 lakh plus cess
She should ask HR to cancel the raise
She should switch to the old regime to avoid the tax
body.explanation: Her taxable income becomes ₹12,25,000. Marginal relief caps tax at the ₹25,000 excess over ₹12 lakh, plus ₹1,000 cess, which is ₹26,000. Her raise is ₹50,000, so she keeps ₹24,000 more. A raise never leaves you with less money.

Tax, interest and penalties once the landlord's PAN is cross-checked

Buying policies or NPS just to reach breakeven
Long lock-ins for little or no net tax saving
Compare the new regime first; invest on merit, not for deductions
Uploading the return on time but e-verifying late
Return treated as late, old regime lost, late fee payable
E-verify the same day you upload
Starting F&O or freelancing without checking the switching rules
Yearly flexibility replaced by one exit and one return
Treat the regime as a multi-year decision once you have business income
Not giving a new employer your previous salary details
Double rebate in TDS and a large bill with interest at filing
Submit previous employer salary and TDS when you join
Deciding once and never reviewing
Missed savings when rent, loans, salary or family change

body.text: Why fake HRA is not worth it. Under the 1961 Act, under-reported income attracted a penalty of 50% of the tax on it, and misreported income, which includes false claims and fabricated evidence, attracted 200%. Rent claims are among the easiest to verify, because the landlord's PAN, their own return and your bank statements all have to line up.

children.text: The Most Expensive Mistake: Chasing the Breakeven

Vikas, a ₹20 lakh sales head in Indore, has ₹6,50,000 of genuine old regime benefits. His breakeven is ₹7,08,333. A colleague tells him to 'just put ₹50,000 into NPS under 80CCD(1B) and the old regime will win'. He does it, locking the money away until he turns 60.

body.title: Vikas Before and After Buying NPS for Tax

columns.label: After: ₹7,00,000 of benefits
points: New regime still cheaper, and ₹50,000 now locked until 60

body.title: How Much Does Vikas Still Overpay?
body.prompt: After the ₹50,000 NPS contribution, if Vikas chooses the old regime, how much more tax does he pay than he would under the new regime?
body.explanation: Old regime taxable income is ₹20,00,000 minus ₹50,000 minus ₹7,00,000, which is ₹12,50,000. Tax is ₹1,12,500 plus 30% of ₹2,50,000 (₹75,000), total ₹1,87,500, plus ₹7,500 cess, which is ₹1,95,000. New regime tax is ₹1,92,400. He pays ₹2,600 more in the old regime, even after locking up ₹50,000. The NPS contribution was still ₹8,333 short of breakeven.

body.text: NPS can be an excellent retirement product. The mistake is buying it, or an endowment plan, or an extra health cover, because of a deduction you have not yet proven you can use. Always run the regime comparison first, then invest for your goals.

body.title: The Family WhatsApp Group
body.scenario: Your cousin Rhea, 26, has just started work in Noida at ₹9 lakh. The family WhatsApp group floods her with advice: her uncle says 'always take the old regime, we salaried people need 80C'; an aunt says 'buy a ₹50,000 LIC policy immediately to save tax'; her brother says 'don't bother filing a return, your company already deducted TDS'; and a friend says 'the regime you pick now is permanent'.
body.prompt: Reply to Rhea with a short correction for each piece of advice.
body.modelAnswer: Uncle: at ₹9 lakh, new regime taxable income is ₹8,25,000, below ₹12 lakh, so her tax is nil. The old regime can at best tie. Aunt: an LIC policy gives no deduction in the new regime, so buy insurance only if she needs cover, and a term plan is usually the cheaper way to get it. Brother: her employer's TDS is likely nil, but she should still file, since filing builds a record for loans and visas, lets her claim refunds on TDS deducted on interest, and she must report any other income that appears in her AIS. Friend: as a salaried employee without business income, she can choose her regime afresh every year in her return, as long as she files by the due date.

body.title: The Business Income Limit
body.textWithBlank: Once a taxpayer with business income opts out of the new regime, they can return to it only ___.
body.explanation: After that single return, they cannot opt for the old regime again while they continue to have business or professional income.

body.title: Myth or Fact? Flip to Check

cards.term: Dividends get the new regime rebate
cards.definition: Fact. Dividends are taxed at slab rates, so the rebate covers them.

cards.term: Short-term gains on shares get the new regime rebate
cards.definition: Myth. Special-rate income is outside the rebate.

cards.term: Employer NPS works in the new regime
cards.definition: Fact. Up to 14% of basic plus DA.

cards.term: Home loan interest is useless in the new regime
cards.definition: Mostly myth. Self-occupied interest is lost, but let-out property interest still reduces rental income.

cards.term: A late return can still choose the old regime
cards.definition: Myth, for taxpayers without business income. A belated return is taxed under the new regime.

cards.term: Gratuity is taxable in the new regime
cards.definition: Myth. Gratuity up to ₹20 lakh is exempt in both regimes.

body.title: Your Annual Regime Review
steps: Every April, list next year's genuine rent, loans, investments and insurance before declaring to payroll
Check whether you have, or plan to have, any business or professional income
Compare your benefits against the breakeven for your expected salary
Every July, rerun the full comparison using Form 16 and AIS
File and e-verify before the due date
Recheck immediately after a job change, home purchase, marriage or a big raise

points: Most regime myths were true under older rules or in narrow cases, but not for most taxpayers in tax year 2026-27.
The ₹12 lakh rebate is for residents and does not cover special-rate capital gains, though it does cover dividends and interest.
Never buy a financial product only to reach breakeven; compare regimes first and invest on merit.
Fake HRA claims are easily detected and can attract heavy penalties.
Late verification, unreported income and undisclosed previous salary are procedural mistakes with real costs.
Review your regime choice every year and after every major life event.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not tax or investment advice. Rules, penalty rates and figures reflect tax year 2026-27 and the Income-tax Act, 1961 provisions as understood at the time of writing, and should be confirmed against the Income-tax Act, 2025. Consult a qualified tax professional before filing.
